title: Find in Mountain Array
description: Brute force to optimized: scanning every index versus a three-phase binary search (find the peak, then search each monotonic side).

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given a mountain array (strictly increasing then strictly decreasing) accessible only through a get(index) API (and a length() API), and a target value, return the minimum index such that the array at that index equals target, or -1 if target does not exist, using as few calls to get() as possible.

blocks.text: The mountain array has exactly one peak; everything before it strictly increases, everything after strictly decreases. Since target could appear on either side of the peak (or not at all), the search must first locate the peak, then search each side with its own appropriate binary search direction.

blocks.title: Analogy: Searching a Hiking Trail's Elevation Log for a Specific Height
blocks.text: Picture a trail log recording elevation as you hike up to a summit and back down. To find where a specific elevation occurred, you would first figure out roughly where the summit is, then search the uphill portion (elevations increasing) or the downhill portion (elevations decreasing) using the appropriate search direction for each.

blocks.caption: Three binary searches: find the peak, then search the increasing side, then the decreasing side

blocks.text: Result: index 2, the minimum index (found on the increasing side, before the peak at index 4).

Before scanning linearly, notice the mountain shape lets binary search locate the peak first (using the same slope-comparison trick as Peak Index in a Mountain Array), and then each side of the peak is individually sorted (one ascending, one descending), letting a direction-appropriate binary search find target on either side.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Finding the peak index first uses the same technique as Peak Index in a Mountain Array: compare arr[mid] to arr[mid+1], moving right if still climbing, left (inclusive) if already descending.

Observation 2: Once the peak is known, the range [0, peak] is strictly increasing, so a standard ascending binary search applies there.

Observation 3: The range [peak, n-1] is strictly decreasing, so a binary search with the COMPARISON DIRECTION REVERSED (since larger values are to the LEFT here) applies there.

Observation 4: Searching the increasing side first (and returning immediately if found) guarantees the MINIMUM valid index is returned, since the increasing side's indices are all smaller than the peak and beyond.

This leads to a three-phase binary search: first find the peak index, then binary search the increasing left side (ascending direction), then if not found, binary search the decreasing right side (descending direction).
Call get(i) for every index from 0 to length-1, comparing each to target directly.

items: Iterate i from 0 to length-1, calling get(i).
If get(i) equals target, return i immediately (guaranteeing the minimum index).
If the loop completes without a match, return -1.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Checking every index directly finds the minimum matching index, guaranteed correct.
This could call get() up to n times, far more than necessary given the mountain structure.

blocks.text: Limitation: the mountain structure allows the peak to be found in O(log n), and each monotonic side searched in O(log n), for O(log n) total calls instead of O(n).

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why scanning every index is wasteful: the mountain shape means the array is really just two sorted sequences glued together at the peak, and both can be binary searched independently once the peak is located.

Finding the peak: use the same slope-comparison binary search as Peak Index in a Mountain Array, comparing arr[mid] to arr[mid+1] to decide direction.

Searching each side correctly: the left side [0, peak] is ascending (standard binary search direction); the right side [peak, n-1] is descending (reversed comparison direction).

Guaranteeing the MINIMUM index: searching the increasing left side FIRST, and only searching the right side if not found there, ensures the smallest valid index is returned, since any match on the left side has a strictly smaller index than the peak and everything after it.

First binary search for the peak index using the slope comparison. Then binary search the increasing range [0, peak] for target; if not found, binary search the decreasing range [peak, n-1] with the comparison direction reversed.

blocks.caption: Find the peak first, then search each monotonic side with the appropriate direction

blocks.text: The peak-finding phase correctly locates the single highest point using the same slope-comparison logic as the simpler Peak Index problem. Once known, the two sides are genuinely, independently sorted (one ascending, one descending), so a direction-appropriate binary search correctly finds target on either side. Searching the increasing side first guarantees that if target appears on both sides (impossible here since values are related to a single peak, but in general searching left first) or only on the left, the minimum index is returned.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(log n) calls to get() (three separate binary searches, each O(log n)).
Space: O(1).

blocks.text: Find in Mountain Array combines two binary search techniques (peak-finding and direction-aware search) into a three-phase solution, minimizing calls to an expensive API.

items: Forgetting to reverse the comparison direction when searching the decreasing (right) side.
Searching the decreasing side FIRST, which could return a valid but non-minimal index if target also appears (or would appear) on the increasing side.

blocks.text: Explicitly breaking this into "first find the peak, then two direction-aware binary searches" clarifies the solution structure and demonstrates comfort composing multiple binary search variants.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "search a mountain-shaped array, minimizing API calls", think: find the peak first, then binary search each monotonic side with the correct direction.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: The linear scan costs O(n) API calls; the three-phase binary search costs O(log n) calls, both using O(1) space.

items: Pattern: a three-phase binary search: find the peak, then search each monotonic side with the correct comparison direction.
Core Idea: locate the peak via slope comparison; binary search the increasing side normally; if not found, binary search the decreasing side with reversed comparisons.
Time: O(n) for the linear scan, O(log n) for the three-phase binary search.
Most Important Observation: a mountain array is really two independently sorted sequences glued at the peak.
Interview Difficulty: a solid combination problem, testing composition of multiple binary search variants.
One line memory trick: find the peak, search up normally, search down with flipped comparisons.
